Atheists
ā´thē-ĭsts
n. pl. (those who deny or live without God; the AV renders the Greek atheoi as “without God in the world”)
Greek a-, without, and theos, God. The one New Testament occurrence is Ephesians 2:12, and it is said of Gentiles who had many gods — which tells us what the Bible means by the word.

Biblical Definition

The Greek atheoi appears once and describes the Ephesians before conversion: they were “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world” (Eph 2:12) — men with a temple of Diana in their city. The denial Scripture treats is practical rather than philosophical: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works” (Psa 14:1; Psa 53:1). Paul's account is of suppression, not ignorance: “when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful” (Rom 1:21). And Jeremiah gives the exchange: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines atheist as one who disbelieves the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being; and atheism as the disbelief of the existence of a God.

expand to see more

ATHEIST, n. One who disbelieves the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being.

2. A godless person.

ATHEISM, n. The disbelief of the existence of a God, or Supreme intelligent Being.

ATHEISTICAL, a. Pertaining to atheism; disbelieving the existence of a God; impious; applied to persons.

Key Scripture

Eph 2:12 — "That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:"

Psa 14:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good."

Rom 1:21 — "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened."

Jer 2:13 — "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Psa 53:1 — "To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, Maschil, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good."

Modern Corruption

Atheism is treated as a modern intellectual position, and Scripture's word for it lands on religious people.

expand to see more

Ephesians 2:12 is the surprise. Paul calls the Ephesians atheoi — godless — and Ephesus was one of the most religious cities in the empire, home to a temple counted among the wonders of the world. They had gods in abundance. What they did not have was God, and the biblical category is therefore not about the number of deities a man affirms but about whether he stands in any relation to the living One. On that definition a great deal of religion is atheism with furniture.

Psalm 14:1 is misquoted constantly by leaving out the location. The fool hath said in his heart — not in a lecture, not in an argument. And what follows is not a refutation but a description of conduct: they are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good. The psalm treats practical atheism as the real problem, which is the thing every believer does whenever he acts as if God were not in the room. On that reading the verse's first application is inside the church, and it was David who wrote it about Israel.

This is not a licence to be dismissive of honest unbelief, and Christians who use the fool of Psalm 14 as a term of abuse have misread the psalm and disobeyed the Lord's warning about that word. Romans 1 says the problem is suppression rather than stupidity, and Jeremiah 2:13 says the man who leaves the fountain does not stop digging — he hews out cisterns, works hard at them, and they hold no water. That is a description of something exhausting and sad rather than contemptible, and it deserves the tone Paul used at Athens: argument, patience, and a real hearing given to the objection.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek atheos (G112), without God; Hebrew nabal (H5036), fool; ein Elohim (H430), there is no God; bor nishbar (H953), a broken cistern.

expand to see more

Greek atheos (G112) — without God, godless; Ephesians 2:12 only.

Hebrew nabal (H5036) — fool, one morally senseless; Psalm 14:1, 53:1, Isaiah 32:6, 1 Samuel 25:25.

Hebrew me'ayan mayim chayyim (H4726) — fountain of living waters; Jeremiah 2:13, 17:13, John 4:10–14.

Usage

"“Without God in the world” — said of men with a temple of Diana."

"“The fool hath said in his heart” — in his heart, and then his conduct."

"“Hewed them out cisterns” — exhausting work, holding no water."
